items.title: Sets inside sets
items.prose: Let $X = \{1, \{1\}, \{1, 2\}\}$. Its elements are the number 1, the set $\{1\}$ and the set $\{1, 2\}$.
items.question: Which are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: You looked inside $\{1, 2\}$. 2 is an element of that element, not of $X$, so $2 \notin X$.
You confused $\in$ with $\subseteq$. $\{1, 2\} \in X$ is true, but $2 \notin X$, so it is not a subset.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the three elements of $X$, then test each statement against that list.

explain.text: $X$ has three elements: 1, $\{1\}$ and $\{1, 2\}$, so $|X| = 3$. $\{1\}$ is both an element and, since $1 \in X$, a subset. But $2 \notin X$, so no set containing 2 is a subset of $X$.

items.title: A difference law
items.prose: Prove $A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)$ for all sets $A$, $B$, $C$ by chasing an element. Each line states its reason.
items.question: Put the proof in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Then $x \in A$ and $x \notin B \cup C$, by the definition of difference.
So $x \in A$, and not ($x \in B$ or $x \in C$), by the definition of union.
So $x \in A$, $x \notin B$ and $x \notin C$, by De Morgan for statements.
So $x \in A \setminus B$ and $x \in A \setminus C$, using $x \in A$ twice, by the definition of difference.
So $x \in (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)$, by the definition of intersection.
Every step is an “if and only if”, so the chain reverses and the sets are equal. $\blacksquare$
So $x \in A$, and $x \notin B$ or $x \notin C$, by De Morgan for statements.
lines.why: You kept “or” when moving “not” inside. Not ($P$ or $Q$) is not $P$ and not $Q$.

feedback.correct: Right. Unpack difference and union, De Morgan, then rebuild.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Unpack the left side one definition at a time, then rebuild the right side.

byKey.d1: You used the line with “or”. It would prove a different set, $(A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. The last line, on reversing, is part of it too.
byKey.s7: The reversal comes last, once the chain reaches the right side.

explain.text: Each line applies one definition or De Morgan for statements. Every step holds both ways, so the chain also runs from right to left. On the sets of Unions, intersections and complements both sides are $\{2, 10\}$.

items.title: The key step
items.prose: In that proof, line 3 reads “$x \in A$, and not ($x \in B$ or $x \in C$)”. Line 4 reads “$x \in A$, $x \notin B$ and $x \notin C$”.
items.question: Which rule takes line 3 to line 4?

options.why: You named a set law. The step works inside the statement, on “not” and “or”.
Difference was used in line 2. No $\setminus$ appears in lines 3 and 4.
No implication is reversed here. Only a negation moves inside an “or”.

feedback.correct: Right. Negating an “or” gives an “and” of negations.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two lines: what happened to “not” and “or”?

explain.text: Line 3 negates an “or”, and line 4 writes it as an “and” of two negations. That is De Morgan for statements, from And, or and not.

items.title: Check it on the diagram
items.prose: Back to $U = \{1, \dots, 12\}$ with $A$ even, $B$ multiples of 3 and $C$ multiples of 4.
items.question: Tap every region of $A \setminus (B \cup C)$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\{2, 10\}$: even, and neither a multiple of 3 nor of 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stay inside $A$ and leave out everything in $B$ or in $C$.

byKey.or: You tapped $(A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)$, the distractor's set $\{2, 4, 6, 8, 10\}$.
byKey.all-a: You kept all of $A$. The numbers in $B$ or $C$ must go.
byKey.AB: 6 is a multiple of 3, so it is in $B \cup C$.
byKey.AC: 4 and 8 are multiples of 4, so they are in $B \cup C$.

explain.text: $B \cup C = \{3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12\}$, so $A \setminus (B \cup C) = \{2, 10\}$. Also $A \setminus B = \{2, 4, 8, 10\}$ and $A \setminus C = \{2, 6, 10\}$, which meet in $\{2, 10\}$. The example agrees with the proof.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $5x - 7 = y$ for $x$, undoing the last step first.

byKey.order: You divided before adding 7. Undo the $-7$ first.
byKey.recip: You read $g^{-1}$ as $1/g$. The $-1$ means the inverse function, not a power.

explain.text: From $5x - 7 = y$, add 7 to get $5x = y + 7$, then divide by 5. So $g^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{y + 7}{5}$. Check: $g\big(\tfrac{y + 7}{5}\big) = (y + 7) - 7 = y$.

byKey.fwd: You worked out $g(8) = 33$. The inverse runs the other way.

items.title: Counting onto functions
items.prose: Four trades are each routed to one of three brokers. Every broker must get at least one trade. That is an onto function from 4 trades to 3 brokers.
items.question: How many onto functions are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Exactly one broker gets two trades. Choose that pair of trades, then deal out the three groups.

byKey.all: You counted every function, $3^4 = 81$, including those that miss a broker.
byKey.no-pair: You counted only how to deal 3 groups to 3 brokers. First choose which 2 trades share a broker: 6 ways.
byKey.perm: You used $4 \times 3 \times 2$, a one-to-one count. Here two trades must share.

explain.text: Onto from 4 to 3 means one broker gets two trades and the others one each. Choose the pair in $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ ways, then give the 3 groups to 3 brokers in $3! = 6$ ways. That is $6 \times 6 = 36$ of the $3^4 = 81$ functions.

items.title: If the composite is one-to-one
items.prose: $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$, with $(g \circ f)(a) = g(f(a))$. Claim: if $g \circ f$ is one-to-one, then $f$ is one-to-one. Nothing is assumed about $g$.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Two lines do not belong: move them to Left out.

lines.text: Let $a, b \in A$ be arbitrary, and suppose $f(a) = f(b)$.
Since $g \circ f$ is one-to-one, $a = b$. So $f$ is one-to-one. $\blacksquare$
Since $g$ is one-to-one, $g(f(a)) = g(f(b))$ gives $f(a) = f(b)$.
lines.why: You assumed $g$ is one-to-one. The claim says nothing about $g$; only $g \circ f$ is one-to-one.
That is the wrong direction. Equal inputs give equal outputs for every function.

feedback.correct: Right. Assume $f(a) = f(b)$, apply $g$, use $g \circ f$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from equal outputs of $f$ and use only what the claim gives.

byKey.d1: You used that $g$ is one-to-one, an extra assumption. The proof must work for any $g$.
byKey.d2: You started from $a = b$. One-to-one needs $f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: We assumed $f(a) = f(b)$ and applied $g$, which any function allows. That gives $(g \circ f)(a) = (g \circ f)(b)$, and the hypothesis on $g \circ f$ gives $a = b$. At no point did we need $g$ to be one-to-one.

items.title: Composing one-to-one functions
items.prompt:
Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$, with $(g \circ f)(a) = g(f(a))$.

(a) Prove: if $f$ and $g$ are both one-to-one, then $g \circ f$ is one-to-one. Give a reason for every line.

(b) Show by a counterexample on small sets that $g \circ f$ can be one-to-one while $g$ is not. Write out $A$, $B$, $C$, $f$ and $g$, and check both claims.
items.model:
**(a)** Let $a_1, a_2 \in A$ be arbitrary, and suppose $(g \circ f)(a_1) = (g \circ f)(a_2)$. We show $a_1 = a_2$.

1. By the definition of $g \circ f$, $g(f(a_1)) = g(f(a_2))$.
2. $g$ is one-to-one, and $f(a_1)$, $f(a_2)$ are elements of $B$, so $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$.
3. $f$ is one-to-one, so $a_1 = a_2$.

As $a_1$ and $a_2$ were arbitrary, $g \circ f$ is one-to-one. $\blacksquare$

**(b)** Take $A = \{1\}$, $B = \{1, 2\}$ and $C = \{1\}$. Let $f(1) = 1$, and let $g(1) = 1$ and $g(2) = 1$.

- $g \circ f : \{1\} \to \{1\}$ sends 1 to $g(f(1)) = g(1) = 1$. Its domain has one element, so no two different inputs exist. It is one-to-one, vacuously.
- $g$ is not one-to-one: $g(1) = g(2) = 1$, but $1 \ne 2$.

The element $2 \in B$ is never an output of $f$, so $g$'s fault there never shows in $g \circ f$. In desk terms: one trader, two desks, and a manager map sending both desks to one floor.

rubric.text: Starts (a) from $(g \circ f)(a_1) = (g \circ f)(a_2)$ for arbitrary $a_1, a_2$ and states the goal $a_1 = a_2$.
Unpacks the composite to $g(f(a_1)) = g(f(a_2))$ and uses that $g$ is one-to-one to get $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$.
Uses that $f$ is one-to-one to get $a_1 = a_2$, and concludes, with a reason on every line.
Gives explicit sets $A$, $B$, $C$ and functions $f$, $g$ for (b), with $g$ not one-to-one.
Checks both claims in (b): $g \circ f$ is one-to-one, and two named inputs share an output of $g$.
